tip.title: depuis, pendant, il y a
tip.body: Three ways to talk about time: depuis + present for something still going on (Je travaille ici depuis deux ans — I've been working here for two years); pendant + passé composé for a finished period (J'ai travaillé pendant trois ans à Lyon); il y a + passé composé for 'ago' (J'ai eu mon diplôme il y a cinq ans). Pronunciation: make the liaison in deux_ans, trois_ans, six_ans, dix_ans (a z sound), and in neuf ans the f becomes a v: neu-v-ans.

lessons.title: The job interview
lessons.goal: Answer typical interview questions about yourself, your strengths and your motivation.

tip.title: L'entretien d'embauche
tip.body: A job interview is un entretien d'embauche (in Québec: une entrevue). Always use vous unless invited to switch. To apply is postuler: postuler à un poste, postuler chez Renault; your application is votre candidature. Strengths and weaknesses are vos points forts and vos points faibles; a classic trick is to present a weakness you are working on. Pronunciation: in entretien the en is nasal and the -tien ends in a nasal 'ti-in'; in disponible all the syllables are clear: dis-po-nibl.

tip.title: Formal set phrases
tip.body: Applications use fixed formulas. In writing: Vous trouverez ci-joint mon CV (Please find my CV attached) and Je reste à votre disposition pour un entretien (I am available for an interview). On the phone, introduce yourself clearly and say why you're calling: Je vous appelle au sujet de l'annonce… CV is said 'cé-vé'.

lessons.title: Qui, que, où
lessons.goal: Join sentences with relative pronouns to describe jobs, people and places.

tip.title: Subject, object or place?
tip.body: qui is the subject of the next verb, so a verb follows it directly: un collègue qui parle anglais. que is the object, so a new subject follows: le poste que je cherche. que becomes qu' before a vowel (le poste qu'il occupe) but qui never changes. où is used for places and also for time: l'entreprise où je travaille, le jour où j'ai commencé. Watch the agreement: with que + passé composé with avoir, the past participle agrees with the noun before it: la lettre que j'ai écrite. Unlike English, French never drops que: the job I want = le poste que je veux.

culture.title: Lettre de motivation, CDI and CDD
culture.body: In France, an application traditionally means a CV plus a lettre de motivation (cover letter), often written in a fairly formal style that ends with a set formula such as « Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées ». Contracts matter a lot: the CDI (contrat à durée indéterminée, open-ended) is the one most people hope for, while a CDD (contrat à durée déterminée) is fixed-term; new jobs usually start with a période d'essai (trial period). In Switzerland, applications often include a full dossier with copies of diplomas and certificats de travail (written references from former employers). In Québec you go to an entrevue and hope for a poste permanent.
